name: Avoiding Common ADU Plan-Check Corrections in Los Angeles

mainEntity.name: What are the most common plan-check corrections Los Angeles homeowners receive for new detached ADUs, and how can I avoid them?
mainEntity.text: What are the most common plan-check corrections Los Angeles homeowners receive for new detached ADUs, and how can I avoid them?

acceptedAnswer.text: City websites outline ADU rules broadly, but they rarely list the practical plan-check issues that slow approvals. For new detached ADUs in Los Angeles, recurring corrections include unclear or non-compliant setbacks from property lines and existing structures, exceeding maximum height or floor area, and misinterpreting parking exemptions. Incomplete or incorrect site plans—missing dimensions, easements, or slopes—also trigger rejections. On the technical side, structural details that lack proper footing, shear, and connection notes, or generic details that do not match your specific design, invite corrections. Energy compliance (Title 24) is another common snag; missing forms, inconsistent window specifications, or unclear insulation values lead to delays. Utility connection plans that fail to show how sewer, water, gas, and power will be routed and metered can also return for revision. To avoid these issues, start with an accurate survey or base map of your lot. Hire a designer, engineer, or design-build contractor experienced with ADUs in your jurisdiction to prepare coordinated architectural, structural, and energy documents. Have them verify current ADU ordinances and internal policy memos, which can change faster than websites. Clear, complete notes about fire-rating, drainage, and utility routing on the initial submittal greatly increase the odds of a faster approval with fewer correction rounds.
acceptedAnswer.description: Frequent ADU plan-check corrections involve parking, setbacks, height, utility connections, and incomplete structural or energy details. Avoid them by confirming current ADU ordinances, using accurate site plans, coordinating utility layouts early, and submitting complete structural, Title 24, and fire notes prepared by professionals familiar with local requirements.
